posts.name: Pony
posts.cooked:
Hi, I’m Pony, founder of Weft. I’m looking to connect with n8n implementers who work on SaaS customer-request workflows across support, product and engineering.

To be clear: I’m validating the service and have no client build to refer yet. This is an exploratory partner introduction, not an open paid job or a promise of work.

Weft’s package covers reviewing one workflow, mapping the current and proposed process, defining owners and required data, and documenting exception paths and acceptance checks. Implementation is separately scoped.

The collaboration I’d like to explore is: Weft prepares the process brief; an implementer checks technical feasibility and, if there is a suitable client project, quotes the build separately. Access, APIs, hosting, monitoring and support responsibilities would need agreement before any build.

For example, a customer update should depend on confirmed release availability for that account, rather than just a task moving to Done. I want the handover brief to explain that rule and what happens when data is missing or a sync fails.

An illustrative sample of the planning deliverable is here: Weft | Sample SaaS workflow improvement blueprint
It is not a client result or an importable n8n workflow.

If this kind of collaboration fits your work, what would you need in a process brief before you could assess and quote it? A short reply about your relevant experience is enough; no unpaid demo or proposal is requested.

Pony
Weft

posts.name: Matt Michels
posts.cooked:
I build n8n and Supabase workflows, so your rule that a customer update should depend on confirmed release availability for that account, not a task moving to Done, is the kind of brief I can assess.

The closest real build is my lead triage pipeline. Python fetchers pull posts on a schedule, dedupe and score them, and an LLM drafts a response. A rule-based validator then checks every draft. A failed draft gets one retry with the exact failure fed back. A second failure goes to a human-review queue with an email alert, and every action is written to an append-only ledger. That is the missing-data and failed-sync handling you describe.

I also run a missed-call text-back line, where a Supabase edge function verifies the Twilio signature, texts the caller back and logs the miss to Postgres.

To be plain, my n8n workflows are self-hosted and test-built on localhost with synthetic data, with no client production. My production automation runs as Supabase edge functions and Python workers.

In a brief I would need the source systems and their APIs, the owner of each step, the required fields, the missing-data and sync-failure paths, and the acceptance checks.

I can walk through the real builds on a live screen-share, and I work about 20 hours a week, US Eastern.

posts.name: mahathir lol
posts.cooked: Hi Pony, adding one thing to the lists above: put 5-10 real (anonymized) examples in the brief, each with the input data and the exact outcome you expect, including the messy ones like missing account data or a sync that fails halfway. Rules are enough to quote from, but examples catch the “oh, that’s not what we meant” moments before the build starts, and they become your acceptance tests. Full disclosure: I’m with Pond AI, we build custom AI agents and workflows around the tools a business already uses. Would you want implementers to see a brief before it goes to the client, or after?

posts.cooked:
Thanks all — the access model, expected volume and exception paths are useful additions to the handover brief. I’ve noted the introductions and the distinction between test-built workflows and production experience.

@mahathir_lol: my intended sequence is to agree the problem and desired outcome with the client first, then involve an implementer before finalizing any technical scope or build estimate. The client can review a draft process map earlier, with unverified integrations clearly marked. A feasibility review or integration test would be separately agreed and scoped, not assumed to be free.

The anonymized input/expected-output examples are a useful addition, especially for missing data and partial failures. They should come from the client with permission and feed into the acceptance checks.

There is still no active client build, so there’s no need for a demo, proposal or further work at this stage. I’ve noted your introductions here and can revisit fit when there is a concrete brief. Thanks for the practical input.

posts.name: Shital Katre
posts.cooked:
CRASH-PROOF SAAS WORKFLOW ORCHESTRATION: VALIDATING THE EXCEPTION PATHS

Hi Pony,

Your approach to separating process discovery from pure node wiring is exactly how enterprise automation should be designed. Moving an account to ‘Done’ based on release availability rather than a loose state mutation requires strict, deterministic data boundaries. A naive sync logic will collapse under concurrency or create severe data drifts if third-party webhooks fail mid-transit.

I am a Senior AI Automation & Backend Infrastructure Architect specializing in transforming probabilistic system layers into crash-proof production realities.

Here is how I architect and validate the exact exception paths your briefs require:
Idempotency & State Protection: To ensure a SaaS customer-request workflow never double-fires during peak sync surges, I deploy native Redis lock primitives (INCR + TTL gates) as atomic idempotency boundaries directly within the data paths. This safely isolates system transitions across 1.2M+ daily external payload vectors.
2. Absolute Structural Determinism: Instead of passing raw JSON bodies between support, product, and engineering tools (Jira, HubSpot, GitHub), I wrap extractions inside hardcoded Pydantic validation schemas. If required data is missing or a sync fails, the exception path triggers an isolated, stateful Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) triage queue rather than throwing an unhandled 500 error.
3. Production Metrics & Telemetry: Every workflow I deploy tracks token consumption and p50/p95 latency from the first execution, backing the network with global Error Trigger loops for instant alerting.

Audit the exact quality, data modeling logic, and crash-proof design of my live configurations straight from my verified GitHub repository:
https://github.com

To assess a Weft process brief, I primarily require: 1) The exact API rate limits & authentication contracts of the target SaaS stack, 2) The deterministic boolean rules for your state transitions, and 3) The boundary parameters for your retry budgets.

I’d love to explore an implementation partnership. Let’s connect via forum DM or drop a sample blueprint my way at: katreshital11@gmail.com

posts.name: Artem Kirpach
posts.cooked:
Your release example is a good one. A ticket in Done usually means the code is merged. It doesn’t tell you the feature is live for that customer’s account, so an update sent on status alone can go out too early. Most of the work is mapping which field or event really means “available for this account”, and what the flow does when the data doesn’t match.

My experience is smaller than a SaaS support/product/engineering setup. I built an n8n flow for a bakery: it reads order emails in Gmail, Gemini pulls out the order details, then it creates a Google Doc, sends a Telegram alert and logs the order in Google Sheets. Same shape on a small scale: messy input, a check, and a message only after the data is confirmed.

To assess and quote, I’d need the brief to cover:

  • trigger and source systems, and whether they have API or webhook access
  • the exact condition for each customer update
  • who handles exceptions
  • where the workflow would be hosted

Would the first pilot start from the support tool or from the issue tracker?

posts.cooked:
Hi @pony_weft , thanks for being upfront that this is exploratory. Your split, Weft writes the process brief and an implementer checks feasibility and quotes the build, is one Pond AI can fit into.

Briefly on experience: Pond AI builds custom AI agents around a client’s own tools, and runs a marketplace where people and AI agents compete on a task and the buyer pays only for results they accept. Each task starts with a written definition of what “done” looks like, which is close to your acceptance checks. Pond AI has 100,000+ users in 150+ countries and has run tasks for teams at ElevenLabs, Google Cloud and GPTZero. Most of that work has been lead generation, people-finding and video, so SaaS customer-request workflows would be new ground, and I’d confirm fit per project.

To your question, here’s what I’d need in a brief before quoting:

  1. Source of truth per state: which system and field confirms “release available for this account”.
  2. Linking IDs: how a request ties to a ticket, a release and an account, and what happens when they don’t match.
  3. Systems and access: APIs, auth, rate limits, and whether a sandbox exists.
  4. Exception paths with owners: missing data, a failed sync, a rollback. Who’s told and what the customer sees.
  5. Send rule: what goes out automatically and what goes to a person first.
  6. Acceptance examples: five to ten real cases with expected outcomes, including one with missing data.
  7. Run and support: who hosts it, who gets alerts, and who fixes failures after delivery.

If a client project comes out of Weft, Pond AI can take the brief and come back with a design and a quote, and the build comes with a 7-day refund.
Disclosure: I’m affiliated with Pond AI.

comments.author: mattmichels
comments.text:
I build n8n and Supabase workflows, so your rule that a customer update should depend on confirmed release availability for that account, not a task moving to Done, is the kind of brief I can assess. 
 The closest real build is my lead triage pipeline. Python fetchers pull posts on a schedule, dedupe and score them, and an LLM drafts a response. A rule-based validator then checks every draft. A failed draft gets one retry with the exact failure fed back. A second failure goes to a human-review queue with an email alert, and every action is written to an append-only ledger. That is the missing-data and failed-sync handling you describe. 
 I also run a missed-call text-back line, where a Supabase edge function verifies the Twilio signature, texts the caller back and logs the miss to Postgres. 
 To be plain, my n8n workflows are self-hosted and test-built on localhost with synthetic data, with no client production. My production automation runs as Supabase edge functions and Python workers. 
 In a brief I would need the source systems and their APIs, the owner of each step, the required fields, the missing-data and sync-failure paths, and the acceptance checks. 
 I can walk through the real builds on a live screen-share, and I work about 20 hours a week, US Eastern.

CRASH-PROOF SAAS WORKFLOW ORCHESTRATION: VALIDATING THE EXCEPTION PATHS 
 Hi Pony, 
 Your approach to separating process discovery from pure node wiring is exactly how enterprise automation should be designed. Moving an account to ‘Done’ based on release availability rather than a loose state mutation requires strict, deterministic data boundaries. A naive sync logic will collapse under concurrency or create severe data drifts if third-party webhooks fail mid-transit. 
 I am a Senior AI Automation & Backend Infrastructure Architect specializing in transforming probabilistic system layers into crash-proof production realities. 
 Here is how I architect and validate the exact exception paths your briefs require: 
  Idempotency & State Protection: To ensure a SaaS customer-request workflow never double-fires during peak sync surges, I deploy native Redis lock primitives (INCR + TTL gates) as atomic idempotency boundaries directly within the data paths. This safely isolates system transitions across 1.2M+ daily external payload vectors. 
2. Absolute Structural Determinism: Instead of passing raw JSON bodies between support, product, and engineering tools (Jira, HubSpot, GitHub), I wrap extractions inside hardcoded Pydantic validation schemas. If required data is missing or a sync fails, the exception path triggers an isolated, stateful Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) triage queue rather than throwing an unhandled 500 error. 
3. Production Metrics & Telemetry: Every workflow I deploy tracks token consumption and p50/p95 latency from the first execution, backing the network with global Error Trigger loops for instant alerting. 
   Audit the exact quality, data modeling logic, and crash-proof design of my live configurations straight from my verified GitHub repository: 
   https://github.com  
 To assess a Weft process brief, I primarily require: 1) The exact API rate limits & authentication contracts of the target SaaS stack, 2) The deterministic boolean rules for your state transitions, and 3) The boundary parameters for your retry budgets. 
 I’d love to explore an implementation partnership. Let’s connect via forum DM or drop a sample blueprint my way at:  katreshital11@gmail.com

Your release example is a good one. A ticket in Done usually means the code is merged. It doesn’t tell you the feature is live for that customer’s account, so an update sent on status alone can go out too early. Most of the work is mapping which field or event really means “available for this account”, and what the flow does when the data doesn’t match. 
 My experience is smaller than a SaaS support/product/engineering setup.  the exact condition for each customer update 
 who handles exceptions 
 where the workflow would be hosted 
 
 Would the first pilot start from the support tool or from the issue tracker?

comments.text:
Hi  @pony_weft  , thanks for being upfront that this is exploratory. Your split, Weft writes the process brief and an implementer checks feasibility and quotes the build, is one Pond AI can fit into. 
 Briefly on experience:  Pond AI  builds custom AI agents around a client’s own tools, and runs a marketplace where people and AI agents compete on a task and the buyer pays only for results they accept. Each task starts with a written definition of what “done” looks like, which is close to your acceptance checks. Pond AI has 100,000+ users in 150+ countries and has run tasks for teams at ElevenLabs, Google Cloud and GPTZero. Most of that work has been lead generation, people-finding and video, so SaaS customer-request workflows would be new ground, and I’d confirm fit per project. 
 To your question, here’s what I’d need in a brief before quoting: 
 
  Source of truth per state:  which system and field confirms “release available for this account”. 
  Linking IDs:  how a request ties to a ticket, a release and an account, and what happens when they don’t match. 
  Systems and access:  APIs, auth, rate limits, and whether a sandbox exists. 
  Exception paths with owners:  missing data, a failed sync, a rollback. Who’s told and what the customer sees. 
  Send rule:  what goes out automatically and what goes to a person first. 
  Acceptance examples:  five to ten real cases with expected outcomes, including one with missing data. 
  Run and support:  who hosts it, who gets alerts, and who fixes failures after delivery. 
 
 If a client project comes out of Weft,  Pond AI  can take the brief and come back with a design and a quote, and the build comes with a 7-day refund. 
Disclosure: I’m affiliated with Pond AI.
